listeningScripts.title: Applying for a Resident's Parking Permit
listeningScripts.text:
Officer: Parking services, Alan speaking.
Caller: Hello, I've just moved into the area and I need a resident's permit.
Officer: I can do that. Can I take your name?
Caller: Yes, it's Imogen Fairweather. Fairweather is F-A-I-R-W-E-A-T-H-E-R.
Officer: And the address you're applying for?
Caller: Twenty-six Bellevue Road.
Officer: Thank you. Which zone is that — do you know?
Caller: I don't, I'm afraid.
Officer: Bellevue Road is zone C. That's the one that operates Monday to Saturday, eight until six. There's no restriction on Sundays.
Caller: Good. What does a permit cost?
Officer: The first permit for a household is sixty pounds a year. A second permit for the same address is a hundred and twenty, deliberately — the higher price is there to discourage second cars in a zone where there aren't enough spaces.
Caller: One is all I need. What do I have to send you?
Officer: Two things. Proof that you live there, which can be a tenancy agreement or a council tax bill, and the vehicle registration document showing your name at that address.
Caller: The registration still shows my old address.
Officer: Then update it first, because I can't accept it as it stands. It usually takes about three weeks.
Caller: That's annoying. Can I park in the meantime?
Officer: Yes — I can issue a temporary permit valid for one month while you sort it out. That's free, but it's issued once only, so don't lose it.
Caller: Thank you, that helps. How long does the full permit take?
Officer: Ten working days from receiving complete documents. It's posted, not emailed, so allow for that.
Caller: And visitors?
Officer: You can buy visitor scratch cards, five pounds for a book of ten, each valid for one day.
Caller: I'll take a book with the application.
Officer: I'll note that. And do read the zone map when it arrives — the boundary runs down the middle of Bellevue Road, and the far side is zone D.

listeningScripts.title: Hall of Residence Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Warden: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Aldergate Hall. I'm Ruth, the residence warden, and this briefing covers the things you'll need in your first week.

Let me start with what most of you will ask about. Your room key is also your building pass, and if you lose it the replacement charge is twenty-five pounds. That charge is not a penalty — it is the cost of recoding every external door, which we have to do, because a lost key that opens the front door is a lost key that opens the front door for anybody.

Laundry is in the basement, and you book a machine through the same app you use for maintenance requests. Do report maintenance through the app rather than telling a member of staff in the corridor: verbal reports get lost, and the app is what generates a job number you can chase.

Kitchens are shared between eight rooms, and this is where most disputes here begin. Our rule is simple — your things go in your cupboard, and anything left on a work surface after ten at night is cleared. I know that sounds severe. It exists because the alternative, which we tried, is a rota that half the corridor ignores and the other half resents.

Now, finding your way. As you come in the main entrance, the porter's lodge is immediately on your right, and that's where parcels are held. The common room is directly opposite, on the left of the entrance. The dining hall is at the far end of the ground-floor corridor, on the north side of the building, and the laundry is directly below it in the basement. Bicycle storage is outside, behind the building, reached through the door at the end of that same corridor. And the study room, which is silent and open all night, is on the first floor above the common room.

One last point, and it is the one I most want you to remember. If you are struggling — with work, money, or anything else — tell somebody in week three, not week thirteen. Almost everything is fixable early and very little is fixable late.

listeningScripts.title: Searching for a Literature Review
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: So, the literature review. Nadia, you said you were having trouble.
Nadia: I searched the database and got eleven thousand results. I don't know where to start.
Tutor: Eleven thousand means your search terms are too broad. What did you type?
Nadia: "Social media and wellbeing."
Tutor: Both of those are enormous. What's your actual question?
Nadia: Whether reducing social media use improves wellbeing in university students.
Tutor: That's much narrower than what you searched for, and it contains the terms you need — an intervention, a population, an outcome. Search for those together rather than for the topic.
Josh: I have the opposite problem. I searched very precisely and got nine results.
Tutor: Nine is too few, and it usually means one of two things. Either the field genuinely is small, which is worth knowing, or you have combined your terms in a way that excludes synonyms. What did the field call this before it was called what you called it?
Josh: I hadn't thought about that.
Tutor: Terminology shifts. Look at the papers you did find, take the keywords their authors used, and search again with those. The references of a good recent review will also give you twenty years of work in an afternoon.
Nadia: How do I know when to stop searching?
Tutor: When new searches return papers you have already seen. That point is real and you will recognise it.
Josh: Should we read everything we find?
Tutor: No. Read titles, then abstracts, then methods, and only then whole papers — and record why you excluded things as you go. If you cannot say why a paper is not in your review, you have not done a review; you have done some reading.
Nadia: That sounds like a lot of record-keeping.
Tutor: It is about twenty minutes a day, and it is the difference between writing the review in a week and reconstructing your own decisions for a month.

listeningScripts.title: Why Re-reading Does Not Work
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: I want to spend this session on how people study, because the methods students overwhelmingly choose are the ones that work least well, and the reason for that is interesting rather than simply careless.

Start with what students do. Surveys of study habits consistently find re-reading at the top — reading the chapter, then reading it again — followed by highlighting and copying out notes. These are the most popular techniques in almost every population studied.

Now the awkward finding. When these are compared with alternatives under controlled conditions, re-reading produces very little durable learning. It reliably produces something else, which is the feeling of learning: the second pass is easier than the first, the material feels familiar, and that fluency is misread as knowing. Students rate themselves as having learned more after re-reading than after methods that in fact teach them more.

The technique that outperforms it is retrieval — closing the book and attempting to recall, or better, testing yourself. This is harder, it feels worse, and the improvement in retention is large. In direct comparisons, students who tested themselves outperform students who re-read on delayed tests, often substantially, while predicting before the test that they will do worse.

That mismatch between what feels effective and what is effective is the central point, and it explains why the better method is not adopted. A student choosing between a technique that feels productive and one that feels like failing is not being lazy; they are using the only signal available to them, and that signal is systematically misleading.

Spacing has a similar profile. The same total study time distributed across several sessions produces markedly better retention than one block, and blocked study feels more coherent while you are doing it. Again the comfortable option is the weaker one.

I will end with the practical version, because it is short. Test yourself rather than review, space the sessions rather than mass them, and mix related topics rather than completing one before starting the next. All three feel worse than the alternatives. That feeling is the cost, and it is worth paying, and no amount of explaining this seems to make the feeling go away — including, I should say, for people who study this for a living.
